concepts.name: Radioactivity, the spontaneous emission of rays by unstable nuclei
concepts.statement: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of some nuclei, which destroys a small part of their mass and emits energetic rays from the nucleus.

concepts.name: Two kinds of evidence that the rays come from the nucleus
concepts.statement: The rays of radioactivity come from the nucleus, not the electrons: they do not vary with chemical state, temperature, pressure or ionization, all of which affect electrons, and each event carries energies of the order of a million electron volts, far beyond atomic energies of a few eV.

concepts.name: Alpha, beta and gamma rays: a helium nucleus, an electron and a photon
concepts.statement: The three kinds of nuclear radiation were named before anyone knew what they were, and the reader must know what each one is. A magnetic field bends alphas and betas in opposite directions and leaves gammas alone, which shows their charges, and later work showed that an alpha is a helium nucleus, a beta is an electron created at the instant of decay, and a gamma is a high-energy photon from a nucleus.

concepts.name: Ionizing radiation, and why its effects and detection follow from ionization
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation is radiation, whether nuclear in origin or not, that ionizes the material that absorbs it. Nuclear decays emit from a few keV to more than 10 MeV per event, while it takes only a few eV to ionize an atom, so the radiation damages tissue and electronics and can be detected.

concepts.name: The range of radiation, and how it depends on energy, material and type
concepts.statement: The range of radiation is the distance it travels through a material. Higher energy gives a greater range, a material dense in electrons gives a smaller one, and at the same energy alphas stop first, betas go farther and gammas farthest, because a greater charge and a lower speed make a particle ionize more readily.

concepts.name: Nuclear radiation
concepts.statement: Nuclear radiation is the rays that originate in the nuclei of atoms, the first examples of which were discovered by Becquerel.

concepts.name: Radioactive
concepts.statement: A substance or object is radioactive when it emits nuclear radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha rays ($\alpha$ rays)
concepts.statement: Alpha rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field as positive charges, later found to be helium nuclei.

concepts.name: Beta rays ($\beta$ rays)
concepts.statement: Beta rays are the kind of nuclear radiation bent by a magnetic field opposite to alpha rays, later found to be electrons created at the instant of decay.

concepts.name: Counting the ion pairs a particle can create from the energy it deposits
concepts.statement: The number of ion pairs a particle can create is the energy it deposits divided by the energy needed to create each pair, which connects the MeV energies of nuclear radiation to the tens of eV of an ionization.

concepts.name: Radiation detectors work directly or indirectly by the ionization radiation creates
concepts.statement: Ionizing radiation cannot be sensed directly, and every radiation detector, from photographic film to a semiconductor, turns the ionization or excitation that radiation produces into something that can be seen or measured.

concepts.name: The Geiger tube counts the current of ion pairs radiation produces in a gas
concepts.statement: In a Geiger tube a voltage between a cylinder and a wire along its axis sweeps up the ion pairs that radiation creates in the gas, and the counter records the brief current as a count. A count does not give the energy, charge or type of the radiation.

concepts.name: Scintillators turn radiation into light, and photomultipliers turn the light into a current
concepts.statement: A second family of detectors records light instead of charge. A scintillator converts the energy of radiation into brief flashes of light, and a photomultiplier multiplies the photoelectrons from each flash at a series of dynodes into a measurable current proportional to the energy deposited. Because the output is proportional, these detectors can tell energy, charge and type as a Geiger tube cannot.

concepts.name: Solid-state detectors convert ionization in a semiconductor directly into a signal
concepts.statement: A semiconductor built to conduct only when ionization frees charge in it acts like a solid Geiger tube, and because it is solid it stops radiation in a short distance and misses few particles. The current is closely related to the energy deposited, so these detectors give sophisticated information as scintillators do.

concepts.name: Radiation detector
concepts.statement: A radiation detector is a device that detects and tracks the radiation from radioactive decay, directly or indirectly through the ionization it creates.

concepts.name: Scintillator
concepts.statement: A scintillator is a radiation detector that records the light produced when radiation interacts with its material.

concepts.name: Photomultiplier
concepts.statement: A photomultiplier is a device that converts light into an electrical signal by multiplying the photoelectrons a flash produces.

concepts.name: Nuclei are made of protons and neutrons, the nucleons
concepts.statement: Nucleons are the particles found inside nuclei, the positive proton and the neutral neutron, with nearly the same mass and both far heavier than an electron.

concepts.name: The unified atomic mass unit and masses in MeV/$c^{2}$
concepts.statement: The unified atomic mass unit is defined so that a neutral $^{12}$C atom has a mass of exactly 12 u, and $1\;\text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg $= 931.5$ MeV/$c^{2}$. A mass in MeV/$c^{2}$ becomes an energy in MeV when multiplied by $c^{2}$.

concepts.name: Writing and reading a nuclide as ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N}$, with $A = N + Z$
concepts.statement: A nuclide is written ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N}$, with the mass number $A$ above, the atomic number $Z$ below, the element symbol, and the neutron number $N$ after it, and with $A = N + Z$ any one of these can be found from the others.

concepts.name: Isotopes, nuclei with the same $Z$ and different $N$
concepts.statement: Isotopes are nuclei with the same $Z$ and different $N$, such as hydrogen, deuterium and tritium. Their chemistry follows $Z$, while their mass and stability follow the whole nucleus.

concepts.name: The radius of a nucleus, $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$
concepts.statement: The radius of a nucleus is $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ with $r_0 = 1.2$ fm, so its volume is proportional to the number of nucleons $A$. This is what happens if nucleons are packed so closely that there is no empty space between them.

concepts.name: Finding the density of nuclear matter
concepts.statement: The density of nuclear matter is found from $r = r_0 A^{1/3}$ and a mass of $A$ u; every nucleus has about the same density, about $2 \times 10^{14}$ times that of water.

concepts.name: The strong and weak nuclear forces, short ranged and much stronger than the Coulomb force
concepts.statement: Two forces act in the nucleus beside the Coulomb force: the strong nuclear force, about 100 times more attractive than the electromagnetic repulsion between protons but falling to zero within a few fm, and the weak nuclear force. Their strength is why nuclear decay energies are so large.

concepts.name: The chart of the nuclides and the pattern of stable nuclei
concepts.statement: The chart of the nuclides plots every known nuclide by $N$ against $Z$. Stable nuclei lie near $N = Z$ for light nuclei and with progressively more neutrons than protons for heavier ones, and nuclei off this band decay toward it.

concepts.name: Magic numbers and the shell structure of the nucleus
concepts.statement: Nuclei with certain numbers of protons or neutrons, the magic numbers, are unusually stable, which means the nucleus has shells as the atom does and closed shells are more stable.

concepts.name: Nucleus
concepts.statement: The nucleus is the region at the center of an atom, consisting of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Neutron
concepts.statement: A neutron is a neutral particle found in the nucleus, with nearly the same mass as a proton.

concepts.name: Nuclide
concepts.statement: A nuclide is a type of atom whose nucleus has specific numbers of protons and neutrons.

concepts.name: Mass number $A = N + Z$
concepts.statement: The mass number $A$ is the number of nucleons in a nucleus, the sum of its neutron number $N$ and its atomic number $Z$.

concepts.name: Neutron number $N$
concepts.statement: The neutron number $N$ is the number of neutrons in a nucleus.

concepts.name: Atomic mass
concepts.statement: The atomic mass is the total mass of the protons, neutrons and electrons in a single atom.

concepts.name: Parent and daughter nuclides, and a decay series
concepts.statement: A decay turns a parent nuclide into a daughter, and a daughter may itself be unstable, so some parents start a whole series of decays that ends only at a stable nuclide, as the $^{238}$U series ends at $^{206}$Pb.

concepts.name: Writing an $\alpha$ decay equation: $Z$ and $N$ each fall by 2
concepts.statement: An $\alpha$ decay equation is written by removing a $^{4}$He nucleus from the parent, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y}_{N-2} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}_{2}$: the daughter is the element two places lower in the periodic table, with a mass number four smaller.

concepts.name: The energy of a nuclear reaction, $E = (\Delta m)c^{2}$
concepts.statement: The energy released in a nuclear reaction comes from the mass destroyed in it, $E = (\Delta m)c^{2}$. When the products have less total mass than the parent, the reaction releases energy and can happen spontaneously; when they have more, it needs an input of energy.

concepts.name: Finding a decay energy from atomic masses, counting the electrons
concepts.statement: A decay energy is found from the atomic masses in the tables, which are those of neutral atoms, so the electrons must be counted. In $\alpha$ and $\beta^{-}$ decay they balance and the atomic masses can be subtracted directly; in $\beta^{+}$ decay two electron masses must also be subtracted.

concepts.name: $\beta^{-}$ decay and the neutrino it requires
concepts.statement: In $\beta^{-}$ decay a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton, and the nucleus creates and emits an electron and an electron’s antineutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y}_{N-1} + \beta^{-} + \bar{\nu}_{e}$. Without the antineutrino, energy, linear momentum and angular momentum would not be conserved.

concepts.name: $\beta^{+}$ decay and electron capture
concepts.statement: Nuclei with too many protons for stability lower $Z$ by one, either by emitting a positron and an electron’s neutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} \to {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y}_{N+1} + \beta^{+} + \nu_{e}$, or by capturing one of their own inner electrons. The two have the same effect on the nucleus.

concepts.name: Conservation of electron family number, and antimatter
concepts.statement: The total number of members of the electron family is constant: electrons and electron’s neutrinos count $+1$ and their antimatter partners count $-1$, so an electron can never be created without an antimatter family member.

concepts.name: Conservation of the total number of nucleons, with conservation of charge
concepts.statement: In every decay the total number of nucleons $A$ is the same before and after, even when protons turn into neutrons or the reverse, and the total charge is conserved as always.

concepts.name: $\gamma$ decay, the emission of photons by an excited nucleus
concepts.statement: In $\gamma$ decay a nucleus left in an excited state falls to lower levels by emitting photons, as an excited atom does, but with MeV energies. $\gamma$ decay does not change the nuclide.

concepts.name: Parent
concepts.statement: The parent is the original nucleus before a decay.

concepts.name: Daughter
concepts.statement: The daughter is the nucleus produced when a parent nucleus decays.

concepts.name: Decay
concepts.statement: Decay is the process by which the nucleus of an unstable atom loses mass and energy by emitting radiation.

concepts.name: Alpha decay ($\alpha$ decay)
concepts.statement: Alpha decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle, a $^{4}$He nucleus.

concepts.name: Beta decay ($\beta$ decay)
concepts.statement: Beta decay is the type of radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits a beta particle, an electron or a positron.

concepts.name: Positron (antielectron)
concepts.statement: The positron, or antielectron, is the antiparticle of the electron, with the electron’s mass and a positive charge; it is emitted in positive beta decay.

concepts.name: Positron decay ($\beta^{+}$ decay)
concepts.statement: Positron decay is the type of beta decay in which a proton in the nucleus is converted to a neutron, releasing a positron and an electron’s neutrino.

concepts.name: Neutrino
concepts.statement: A neutrino is an electrically neutral, weakly interacting elementary particle.

concepts.name: Electron’s neutrino $\nu_e$
concepts.statement: The electron’s neutrino is the neutrino of the electron family, an elementary particle with no net electric charge.

concepts.name: Electron’s antineutrino $\bar{\nu}_e$
concepts.statement: The electron’s antineutrino is the antiparticle of the electron’s neutrino.

concepts.name: Antimatter
concepts.statement: Antimatter is matter composed of antiparticles, each with the same mass as its partner and the opposite charge.

concepts.name: Decay series
concepts.statement: A decay series is a chain of decays in which each daughter is itself unstable and decays in turn, until a stable nuclide is produced.

concepts.name: Electron capture
concepts.statement: Electron capture is the process in which a proton-rich nuclide absorbs one of its own inner atomic electrons and emits an electron’s neutrino, ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}_{N} + e^{-} \to {}^{A}_{Z-1}\text{Y}_{N+1} + \nu_{e}$.

concepts.name: Half-life, the time in which each nucleus has a 50% chance of decaying
concepts.statement: The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time in which each nucleus has a 50% chance of decaying, whatever its history. A large sample falls to half in one half-life, to a quarter in the next, and so on.

concepts.name: The number of nuclei left, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$
concepts.statement: The number of radioactive nuclei left at any time is $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, an exponential decay that halves in each half-life.

concepts.name: The decay constant, $\lambda = 0.693/t_{1/2}$
concepts.statement: The decay constant $\lambda$ sets how fast the exponential decay falls, and it is related to the half-life by $\lambda = 0.693/t_{1/2}$: the shorter the half-life, the larger $\lambda$.

concepts.name: Dating an object from the fraction of a radioactive nuclide left in it
concepts.statement: An age is found from the fraction $N/N_0$ of a radioactive nuclide left in an object and its half-life, given the starting abundance. Carbon-14 dating reaches back 50 or 60 thousand years, and $^{238}$U dating billions of years.

concepts.name: Activity, the rate of decay $R = \Delta N/\Delta t$, in becquerels and curies
concepts.statement: The activity $R = \Delta N/\Delta t$ of a source is its rate of decay, the number of decays per unit time, measured in becquerels or curies.

concepts.name: The activity of a source, $R = 0.693N/t_{1/2}$
concepts.statement: The activity of a source grows with the number of radioactive nuclei and falls with their half-life, $R = 0.693N/t_{1/2}$.

concepts.name: Activity falls exponentially too, $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$
concepts.statement: Since activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei, it falls exponentially along with them, $R = R_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, by half in each half-life.

concepts.name: Becquerel, $1\;\text{Bq} = 1$ decay/s
concepts.statement: The becquerel is the SI unit of activity, one decay per second.

concepts.name: Curie, $1\;\text{Ci} = 3.70 \times 10^{10}$ Bq
concepts.statement: The curie is a unit of activity equal to the activity of 1 g of $^{226}$Ra, $3.70 \times 10^{10}$ Bq.

concepts.name: Radioactive dating
concepts.statement: Radioactive dating is the use of radioactive decay to determine the age of a material from the amount of a radioactive nuclide left in it.

concepts.name: Carbon-14 dating
concepts.statement: Carbon-14 dating is a radioactive dating technique based on the decay of carbon-14, whose abundance in living tissue is fixed until the organism dies.

concepts.name: Binding energy, the energy needed to take a nucleus completely apart
concepts.statement: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy required to completely disassemble it into separate protons and neutrons. The more tightly a nucleus is bound, the larger its binding energy.

concepts.name: The mass defect: a bound nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons
concepts.statement: Pulling a nucleus apart puts energy in, and that energy appears as extra rest mass of the separated pieces. So a nucleus has less mass than its protons and neutrons would have apart, by $\text{BE}/c^{2}$. This is why the products of a spontaneous decay have less mass than the parent.

concepts.name: Calculating BE and BE/$A$ from atomic masses
concepts.statement: The binding energy of a nucleus is found from atomic masses as $\text{BE} = \{[Zm({}^{1}\text{H}) + Nm_{\text{n}}] - m({}^{A}\text{X})\}c^{2}$, and dividing by $A$ gives the binding energy per nucleon.

concepts.name: The binding energy per nucleon peaks near $A = 60$
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon averages about 8 MeV, rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near $A = 60$ and falls slowly for heavy ones, with spikes at especially tightly bound nuclei such as $^{4}$He. The larger BE/$A$, the more stable the nucleus.

concepts.name: Why BE/$A$ falls for heavy nuclei: short-ranged attraction against long-ranged repulsion
concepts.statement: The nuclear force is strong but short ranged, so beyond about $A = 60$ a new nucleon feels only its neighbors, while the Coulomb repulsion reaches every proton. Repulsion grows as nuclei get heavier and nuclear attraction does not, so BE/$A$ falls, and heavy stable nuclei carry extra neutrons.

concepts.name: Binding energy per nucleon, BE/$A$
concepts.statement: The binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons; it reveals the details of the nuclear force, and the larger it is, the more stable the nucleus.

concepts.name: A particle bound in a well cannot, classically, get over the rim
concepts.statement: Nucleons are bound in the nucleus as a marble sits in a bowl: they move about but lack the energy to get over the rim, and outside the rim the Coulomb repulsion would push an $\alpha$ away. Classically such a particle stays trapped forever.

concepts.name: Quantum mechanical tunneling through a potential barrier
concepts.statement: A quantum particle's wave function does not stop at a barrier but decreases exponentially inside it, so a small part of it reaches the other side, and the particle has a small probability of being found there. It goes from one side to the other without ever being in between. The thinner the barrier, the greater the chance, which is why tunneling is negligible for anything classical.

concepts.name: $\alpha$ decay happens by tunneling, and more energetic $\alpha$ decays have shorter half-lives
concepts.statement: An $\alpha$ particle escapes the nucleus by tunneling through the barrier. A more energetic $\alpha$ meets a thinner barrier and escapes more readily, so its half-life is shorter, across 17 orders of magnitude.

concepts.name: Electrons tunnel between a probe and a surface in a scanning tunneling microscope
concepts.statement: Electrons can tunnel across a thin gap between two objects, and because the probability is extremely sensitive to the thickness, the current between a probe and a surface in a scanning tunneling microscope reveals surface features as small as single atoms.
